summary: Discusses architectural implications of IP anycast and gives a historical analysis of its use by IETF protocols. It is informational and does not define a protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: Many houses share one address and the nearest answers. This looks at pros and cons.

questions: history of anycast in ietf protocols
how does anycast differ from unicast
subtitle: Delivering services from multiple locations using the same IP address.

tldr.problem: Some critical Internet services like DNS need to be available in multiple locations while being reachable through a single address. This creates architectural challenges not found in traditional unicast addressing.
tldr.mechanism: IP anycast makes a single service address available at multiple, discrete locations. Packets to that address are routed to the closest location as determined by routing topology, allowing distributed service delivery.
tldr.outcome: Anycast enables resilient, distributed services such as DNS root servers, but introduces complexity with stateful protocols like TCP and requires careful operational management.

facts.label: Appearances of anycast term
facts.value: 176 RFCs and 144 active Internet-Drafts (as of RFC 7094)

today: RFC 7094 is an Informational document describing how IP anycast is used in the Internet. Anycast remains a specialized technique limited to services where the design constraints can be satisfied, particularly DNS services and NTP. It is not a general-purpose service distribution mechanism.

sections.title: What is IP Anycast
sections.content:
IP anycast is a network technique where the same service address is made available at multiple, physically distinct locations. Routers forward packets to one of the available locations based on standard destination-based routing, typically delivering to the topologically closest instance. Unlike unicast (one-to-one) or multicast (one-to-many), anycast is one-to-one-of-many.

Anycast addresses are syntactically indistinguishable from unicast addresses. The key difference is that multiple systems assert reachability for the same address from different locations, a practice considered an error in unicast but normal in anycast. Load-balancing techniques may also distribute traffic among multiple equal-cost paths to different instances.
sections.plainLanguage: An anycast address is like a universal mailbox number. When you send a letter to that number, the postal system figures out which of the many mailboxes with that number is closest to you, and it goes there.

sections.title: Anycast Use in Internet Services
sections.content:
Anycast has been used in Internet services for over two decades. Early experiments in the 1990s tested anycast for service discovery. The first formal specification, RFC 1546, appeared in 1993. By the early 2000s, anycast became well established for DNS services. As of 2014, at least ten of the thirteen DNS root name servers used anycast. Today it is also deployed for other services such as Network Time Protocol (NTP).

The DNS case is particularly significant: RFC 3258 formalized using anycast for distributing authoritative name servers. Since DNS queries are mostly stateless UDP transactions, anycast works naturally. By 2007, the use of anycast was growing for other applications and continues to expand.
sections.plainLanguage: IP anycast has been used successfully for many years. The main success story is DNS root servers, which handle billions of queries daily. When you ask where a website is, your question goes to the nearest DNS root server, wherever that is.

sections.title: Safe Uses and Design Constraints
sections.content:
Anycast works best when applications follow specific design rules. For anycast as a destination address, the safest approach requires: a self-contained request in a single packet, stateless transport like UDP, replies sent to a unicast address, no server state across requests, and idempotent retries. Under these constraints, traffic to an anycast address can safely be routed to different instances without breaking the application.

Using anycast as a source address is riskier. Replies sent to an anycast source address may reach a different instance than the original sender. This works only if the application has private state synchronization between instances or expects distributed replicas. The key constraint for source-address anycast is that reverse path forwarding (RPF) checks must be configured to allow the anycast address to be reachable.
sections.plainLanguage: Anycast works best with simple, quick requests like DNS queries. Problems arise with long conversations (like web sessions) unless the servers are set up to coordinate with each other. It is important that requests be independent; if your request reaches a different server the second time, things should still work.

sections.title: Architectural Problems
sections.content:
Anycast introduces several challenges absent in unicast. The biggest issue is compatibility with stateful transports like TCP. If packets in the same TCP connection are routed to different servers, the connection resets because the new server has no state for that session. Firewalls and middleboxes add complexity: translating an anycast destination to a unicast server address may create new state in the middlebox that does not follow the server change.

Scaling global anycast is another concern. Each anycast service requires at least one route in the global routing table. Multiple anycast services can share a route only if all instances are collocated and the prefix is announced identically from all locations. Operational complexity is high: operators must decide whether to withdraw anycast routes when a service fails, and must carefully scope route announcements to prevent unintended traffic patterns.

Security considerations include the risk of traffic hijacking: if an attacker can inject a route for an anycast address, they can redirect traffic to their server. Unlike multicast, anycast allows one node to intercept traffic intended for others.
sections.plainLanguage: There are tricky problems. Long conversations (like downloading a big file over TCP) break if routed to different servers. It is also hard for networks using anycast to grow, because each service needs its own spot in the routing system. An attacker could pretend to be an anycast server and steal traffic.

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content:
Operating anycast services requires careful management. Service discovery can use anycast: a client sends a discovery request to an anycast address, receives a unicast reply with the actual server address, then connects to that unicast address for the transaction. This adds one round-trip delay but solves many problems.

For DNS specifically, operators must decide on failure handling: whether to withdraw routes when a server fails or rely on DNS failover. RFC 4786 (BCP 126) provides detailed guidance on operating anycast services and concludes that route withdrawals should be coordinated with service availability. Operators should also consider whether to use unique origin Autonomous System Numbers (ASNs) per anycast node to allow fine-grained control and monitoring.

On-link anycast (within a subnet) using IPv6 Neighbor Discovery is more reliable than global anycast because all instances are on the same link and address resolution handles the selection. Off-link anycast (the traditional method) relies entirely on routing dynamics and is less predictable.
sections.plainLanguage: Running anycast services is complex. The best way is to find the nearest server first (anycast discovery), then talk to it over a normal unicast connection. Network operators need to plan carefully for when a server breaks, and decide whether to tell the network to stop using it.

sections.title: Today and the Future
sections.content:
IP anycast is used today for critical Internet services, particularly DNS root servers and TLD operators, as well as for NTP and some content delivery networks. However, it remains limited to services where the architectural constraints can be met or where the benefits clearly outweigh the operational burden. The Internet Architecture Board concluded that global anycast will likely remain limited to a small number of key uses.

Applications considering anycast should carefully evaluate whether the service design meets the safe-use criteria. For most applications, layering anycast only for service discovery (with unicast for actual transactions) is the most practical approach. As networks continue to evolve, anycast remains a useful but specialized tool rather than a general solution for service distribution.
sections.plainLanguage: Today, anycast is mainly used for DNS and a few other critical services. It works well for them because they use quick, stateless queries. For most other things, it is easier to find a server address first (using anycast), then have a normal connection to it.
